## Introduction 

In this notebook, we are reverse engineering the story, [Thousands of kids are missing from school. Where did they go?](https://projects.apnews.com/features/2023/missing-children/index.html)

## Load libraries

Loading required libraries for this analysis.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
  options(scipen=999)
  library(tidyverse)
  library(janitor)
  library(dplyr)

```

## Load and Cleaning Data

In this section, describe the source of the data, write a basic data dictionary for data you are working with, and discuss any caveats or issues you discovered working with this data. 

```{r}
# Load required data

age_pop <- read.csv("data/population-by-age.csv") |> clean_names()
public_enrollment <- read.csv("data/public-enrollment-by-grade.csv") |> clean_names()
private_enrollment <- read.csv("data/private-enrollment-by-grade.csv") |> clean_names ()

# Path to data should be loaded from folder "data" i.e. read_csv("data/name_of_data.csv")

# Clean required data and prepare for analysis if needed. 

clean_public_enrollment <- public_enrollment |> rename(state_ab = "st", public_enrollment = "enrollment")

clean_private_enrollment <- private_enrollment |> 
  rename( private_enrollment = "enrollment", state_ab = "state")

school_story <- clean_public_enrollment |> full_join(clean_private_enrollment, join_by(fips, sch_year, grade, state_ab)) |>
  filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12))
  

```

## Sentences to Engineer
In this notebook, we are reverse engineering five sentences from the story.

### Sentence 1

* **Sentence text**:  “The population of school-age kids in the states we studied fell by about 183,000, according to census estimates.” 

* **Analysis summary**: Our results confirmed the AP's claim that the population of school-age kids in the 22 states studied fell by about 183,000. We found this number by comparing the provided age and population data from July 2020 to the age and population data we have from July 2021. 


```{r}
# Put code to reverse engineer sentence here
twenty_age_pop <- age_pop |>
  mutate(year=year(est_date), month = month(est_date)) |>
  filter(year == 2020 & month == 4) |>
 filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12)) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(total_pop_20=sum(population))

twenty_one_age_pop <- age_pop |>
  mutate(year=year(est_date), month = month(est_date)) |>
  filter(year == 2021 & month ==7) |>
 filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12)) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(total_pop_21=sum(population))

 # rename(twenty="2020", twenty_one="2021") |>
 # mutate(change = twenty_one - twenty ) |>
 # mutate(total_change=sum(change)) |>
 # arrange(desc(change))
  

# twenty_age_pop<- age_pop |>   mutate(year=year(est_date)) |>
 # filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12) & (year == 2020)) |> group_by(year) |> summarize(total=sum(population))

# twenty_one_age_pop<- age_pop |>   mutate(year=year(est_date)) |>
 # filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12) & (year == 2021)) |> group_by(year) |> summarize(total=sum(population))

combo_age_year_change <- twenty_one_age_pop |>
  left_join(twenty_age_pop, join_by(state)) |>
  mutate(change = total_pop_20 - total_pop_21) |>
```

### Sentence 2

* **Sentence text**: "Those states saw private-school enrollment grow by over 100,000 students."
* **Analysis summary**: Our results confirmed the AP’s claim that private school enrollment in the 22 states studied grew by over 100,000 students. The AP article also states that private school enrollment grew by “about 103,000 students.” We found this number by comparing total private school enrollment in the 22 states studied between the 2019-2020 and the 2021-2022 school years. This gives us a difference of 102,847 which explains both sentences where this number is referenced in the AP’s story. 

```{r}
# Put code to reverse engineer sentence here

# private_2020 <- private_enrollment |>
 # filter(sch_year == "2019-2020") |>

 # group_by(fips) |>
 # summarize(enrollment_total = sum(enrollment))

  filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12)) |>
  filter(str_detect(grade, "k_12_total")) |>
  filter(sch_year == "2019-2020" | sch_year == "2021-2022") |>
  group_by(sch_year) |>
 summarize(total_enrollment = sum(enrollment))
```

### Sentence 4

* **Sentence text**: “An analysis by The Associated Press, Stanford University’s Big Local News project and Stanford education professor Thomas Dee found an estimated 230,000 students in 21 states whose absences could not be accounted for. These students didn’t move out of state, and they didn’t sign up for private school or home-school, according to publicly available data.”
* **Analysis summary**: Here, we are finding the 230,000 unaccounted for students the AP described. We then used the available enrollment changes data to find homeschool enrollment growing by over 180,000, which is mentioned in the article. Subtracting the enrollment changes from homeschool, private, and public while also accounting for the drop in population left us with 234,213, which is very close to the number of unaccounted students mentioned in the article.

```{r}
# Put code to reverse engineer sentence here
enrollment_changes <- read_csv("~/Desktop/JOUR/GitHub/FALL26-JOUR772-Assignments-GRAY/major_assignments/reverse_engineering/data/enrollment-changes.csv") |>
  clean_names()

homeschool_enrollment <- enrollment_changes |>
   filter(fips %in% c(6, 36, 22, 37, 53, 8, 13, 27, 55, 33, 25, 30, 10, 38, 11, 46, 45, 31, 44, 47, 42, 12)) |>
    filter(enrollment_type=="Homeschool enrollment") |>
    select(fips, state_abbrev, total_change) |>
  summarize(total_enrollment=sum(total_change))
  

# Display results of code below this codeblock

homeschool_enrollment

```

### Sentence 5

* **Sentence text**: “States where kindergarten is optional were more likely to have larger numbers of unaccounted-for students, suggesting the missing also include many young learners kept home instead of starting school.”
* **Analysis summary**: [Write up two to three sentences describing the results of your analysis.  Were you able to confirm the finding? If not, why not?]

```{r}
# Put code to reverse engineer sentence here

missing_kids_analysis <- read_csv("~/Desktop/JOUR/GitHub/FALL26-JOUR772-Assignments-GRAY/major_assignments/reverse_engineering/data/missing_kids_analysis.csv") |> clean_names() |>   mutate(kindergarten_required = if_else(state_abbrev == "MA", "No", kindergarten_required))

 #missing_kids_analysis |> 
  #group_by(kindergarten_required) |>
  # summarize(total_changes=sum(residual_d_e_f_g)) |>
  # arrange(desc(total_changes))

 # states_kindergarten <- missing_kids_analysis |> 
 # group_by(kindergarten_required) |>
# summarize(count=n()) 

kindergarten_missing_kids <- missing_kids_analysis |> 
  mutate(kids_loss = case_when(
    str_detect(residual_d_e_f_g, "-") ~ "YES",
    .default = "NO")) 
  
  
  

kindergarten_missing_kids |> 
  group_by(kindergarten_required) |>
  summarize(
    total_school_count  = n(),
    schools_with_kids_loss = sum(kids_loss == "YES", na.rm = TRUE),
    probability_kids_loss = schools_with_kids_loss / total_school_count
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(probability_kids_loss))
```
